--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.betweenness_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Calculate betweenness centrality scores for all nodes. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.betweenness_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Calculate betweenness centrality scores for all nodes. title: >- [Graph.betweenness_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Calculate betweenness centrality scores for all nodes. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate betweenness centrality scores for all nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L49892-L50044){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.betweenness_centrality( weighted=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Betweenness centrality](../assets/graphs/betweenness-centrality.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same seven-node strip of triangles with a tail, shaded by betweenness. Bridge node E lies on every shortest path between the triangles and the tail F, G, so it tops the table at 0.53, ahead of the hub C and the tail node F at 0.33; A and G score 0." width="100%"} Betweenness centrality measures how often a node appears on the shortest paths between other nodes in the graph. Nodes with high betweenness act as bridges or bottlenecks, controlling the flow of information or resources through the network. This metric is particularly useful for: - identifying key connectors in social networks - finding critical infrastructure nodes in transportation/communication networks - detecting potential bottlenecks or points of failure The algorithm computes shortest paths between all pairs of nodes and counts how many times each node appears on these paths. On a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`), "shortest" means lowest total edge weight, found with Dijkstra's algorithm, so that betweenness agrees with `shortest_path()`; on an unweighted graph it means fewest hops. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to measure distances by edge weight. If `None` (default), follows the graph: weights are used on a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`) and hop counts otherwise, the same rule `shortest_path()` uses. Pass `True` or `False` to override. Edges without a weight count as `1.0`; weights must be non-negative. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store betweenness scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `betweenness_centrality`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to betweenness scores (range of `[0, 1]`). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~edge_betweenness_centrality`) : The same count for edges. [](`~load_centrality`) : A close relative that splits paths evenly at each step. [](`~betweenness_centrality_subset`) : Count only paths between chosen sources and targets. [](`~current_flow_betweenness_centrality`) : Count all paths, not only the shortest. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A node that joins two halves of a graph sits on every shortest path between them. In a five-node path, the middle node carries the routes between the two nodes on each side of it, and the ends carry none: ::: {#0b1a3aa2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec line = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(n=5) line.betweenness_centrality().get_node_df().select( "label", "betweenness_centrality" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 2)
labelbetweenness_centrality
strf64
"1"0.0
"2"0.5
"3"0.666667
"4"0.5
"5"0.0
``` ::: ::: ### The Medici The marriages between the leading families of Renaissance Florence are a classic case. The Medici had more marriage ties than any other family, but not overwhelmingly more: ::: {#3b67333d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} florentine = ec.florentine_families().betweenness_centrality() ( florentine.get_node_df() .select("label", "degree", "betweenness_centrality") .sort("betweenness_centrality", descending=True) .head(6) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (6, 3)
labeldegreebetweenness_centrality
stri64f64
"Medici"60.521978
"Guadagni"40.254579
"Albizzi"30.212454
"Salviati"20.142857
"Ridolfi"30.113553
"Bischeri"30.104396
``` ::: ::: The Medici have half again as many ties as the Guadagni or the Strozzi, but twice the betweenness of any other family: a little over half of the shortest routes between the other families pass through them. The Strozzi, with as many ties as the Guadagni, are seventh, because the families they married into were already connected to each other. Sizing and coloring the families by the score makes the brokers stand out: ::: {#326bba71 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} florentine.plot( size_by="betweenness_centrality", color_by="betweenness_centrality", label_by="label", seed=5, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### Hops or minutes On a weighted graph, the shortest route is the one with the lowest total weight. The metro is weighted by travel time, so betweenness counts the fastest routes; with `weighted=False` it counts the routes with the fewest stops: ::: {#b720db07 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro = ( ec.metro() .betweenness_centrality() .betweenness_centrality(weighted=False, attr_name="by_stops") ) ( metro.get_node_df() .select("label", "betweenness_centrality", "by_stops") .sort("betweenness_centrality", descending=True) .head(5) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 3)
labelbetweenness_centralityby_stops
strf64f64
"Market"0.3791420.318324
"Eastfield"0.3118910.298635
"Riverside"0.2807020.331189
"Central"0.2748540.173099
"Museum"0.2495130.181287
``` ::: ::: Riverside lies on the most fewest-stops routes, but Market on the most fastest ones: the downtown links through Market are quicker, so trips that could go either way go through Market. Central drops from fourth to seventh when stops are counted instead of minutes. Colored by the minutes-based score, the map shows the fastest routes funneling through Market and Eastfield on the way east: ::: {#7bd0463d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro.plot(layout="pos", color_by="betweenness_centrality", label_by="label") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: For the edges that carry the most routes, use `edge_betweenness_centrality()`; for large graphs where an estimate will do, `approximate_current_flow_betweenness_centrality()` samples instead of using every pair.
